newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HORSE RACING-AUSTRALIAN JOCKEY GARY MOORE TO RETIRE AT 45.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-AUSTRALIAN JOCKEY GARY MOORE TO RETIRE AT 45.

text.p: Globe-trotting Australian jockey Gary Moore said on Tuesday that he is to retire after booting home more than 1,000 winners in 10 countries.
The 45-year-old rider ranked riding for his family -- father George and brother John -- and winning the 1981 Prix de L'Arc de Triomphe in Paris on Gold River as two great career highlights.
"But being champion jockey of France in 1987 must be the most distinguished award of my career," he told Reuters after announcing that he is to hang up his boots next weekend.
"I am going to retire on Sunday. I felt it is an appropriate day as I am representing (the Portuguese enclave of) Macau in an international jockey series," he said.
Moore, who has won 20 Group One races around the world, said he had not taken the decision lightly and wanted to quit while he is ahead.
"I wanted to go out on a high and there are other things I would like to do with my life. But I would find it very difficult to follow in my father and brother's footsteps as a trainer," he said.
Moore, rapidly counting up the 10 countries he has ridden in from Sweden to Japan, has clocked up 1,004 winners around the globe and is still hopeful of making a triumphant farewell in Macau.
It has certainly been a seesaw career. He was banned from racing worldwide in 1990 for betting-related offences in a case that shook Hong Kong racing to its roots.
Moore, whose big race victories range from a French Derby to the English and French 1,000 Guineas, had always pledged he would return to Hong Kong after the ban was lifted.
"After being disqualified in 1990, I always vowed that I would ride again in Hong Kong for my fans. I have fulfilled my goal," he said.
Moore, eight times champion jockey in Hong Kong, has been based in Macau since returning to race riding two years ago.
He revealed that he had been pondering his future since scoring on Victory Mount on Queen Elizabeth Cup Day in Hong Kong in April.

"Hong Kong racing ranks among the most successful in the world. The turnover at last weekend's meeting was a world record," he said of the colony whose racing went out on an end-of-seaon high before the June 30 handover to China.
